claims.text: Catalytic performance in nanoscale platinum-group-metal ethanol-oxidation catalysts is governed by formation of a controlled sub-monolayer surface oxide.
The sub-monolayer oxide tunes the adsorption strength of reaction intermediates.
The oxide promotes balanced activation of ethanol and water.
Balanced activation of ethanol and water promotes complete 12-electron ethanol oxidation and enhances activity, selectivity, and durability.
The initial catalyst is a pristine nanoscale platinum-group-metal catalyst with minimal oxide coverage.
Applying a controlled anodic potential will generate a limited sub-monolayer surface oxide.
A sufficiently low baseline potential prevents significant oxide formation.
The relevant structural mediator is surface-bound platinum oxide or an analogous PGM-oxide species.
Sub-monolayer oxide optimizes adsorption energies for both ethanol and water.
Optimized adsorption facilitates the electron and proton transfers required for complete 12-electron oxidation.
Minimal oxide coverage produces less-optimal adsorption and lower catalytic activity and durability.
Operation at the oxide-forming potential will yield higher ethanol-oxidation rates than operation at the baseline potential.
Operation at the oxide-forming potential will improve selectivity toward complete oxidation products such as CO2.
Operation at the oxide-forming potential will increase catalyst durability.
Oxide formation beyond the optimal sub-monolayer coverage will decrease catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism applies under aqueous ethanol-oxidation conditions with potential control.
The same performance trend may fail under non-aqueous conditions or at elevated temperatures because oxide-formation kinetics differ.
The optimal oxide coverage has not been precisely determined.
Variation in the interplay between oxide formation and electronic-structure modification may alter the catalytic enhancement.
Failure to observe a statistically significant improvement or a correlation between sub-monolayer oxide coverage and performance would falsify the hypothesis.
